Corpus › Declarations › kernel

kernel

Translation status: English reader-locale proof. Term names and code fences follow the en pack; supporting prose may still be English.

Sugar @ kernel fragment modifier marks a fragment-shader entry on the kernel surface.

Syntax: @ kernel fragment

Category#

lane

Related#

  • nucleum
  • annotation-sugar

Examples#

radix/corpus/annotation-sugar/nucleum-fragment.fab (canonical · annotation)#

Sugar @ kernel fragment modifier marks a fragment-shader entry on the kernel surface.

# =============================================================================
# kernel — sugar @ kernel fragment modifier
# =============================================================================
#
# What this teaches:
#   • Sugar modifier — `@ kernel fragment` on a function declaration marks
#     it as the fragment-shader entry (NucleumRole::Fragment); the parser
#     reads `fragment` as structured modifier data on the kernel annotation,
#     never as an untyped name/argument pair
#   • The la reader spelling — `kernel` is the la surface of the kernel
#     annotation identity; the en twin is `@ kernel fragment`
#   • A marked fragment function is a systems/shaders entry, not a host
#     entry — the plain `main` driver below proves the module still
#     checks and runs on the host lane
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • writing `@ fragment` alone — the bare fragment name stays the graphics
#     statement annotation, not the kernel modifier
#   • expecting the marked function to be called from a host `main`
#
# See also: kernel, annotation-sugar
# =============================================================================

@ kernel { fragment = true }
fn umbra() → void {
}

fn identitas(int x) → int {
    return x
}

main {
    print identitas(5)
}

Expected output:

5

radix/corpus/kernel/legality-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

Kernel legality at check time: host output, host-only types, calls to non-kernels, host calls to private kernels, and raw thread-id calls are named diagnostics.

# =============================================================================
# kernel — kernel legality is decided by `faber check`
# =============================================================================
#
# What this teaches:
#   • A kernel body must not need the host runtime: no console output, no
#     conversations, no async or generator forms, no heap-backed values
#     (`list`, `map`, `set`, `string`, `json`, `value`), no local handlers.
#   • A kernel may call another kernel or a built-in device operation, never
#     an ordinary function.
#   • Only a public kernel is launchable: host code may call a public kernel
#     but not a private one.
#   • A kernel never names its own lane: the thread-id builtins
#     (`global_invocation_id()` and its siblings) are raw lane ids and are
#     rejected in user code; the parallel pattern is an `for … at`
#     loop over the tensor.
#   • Each violation is a named diagnostic on the offending line, reported
#     by `faber check` before any device lowering runs.
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • printing from a kernel to debug it — run the kernel on the runner
#     oracle instead.
#   • passing a `list` to a kernel — use a tensor.
#
# See also: kernel, public
# =============================================================================

fn host_double(f32 x) → f32 {
    return x * 2.0
}

# 1. host output
@ kernel
@ public
fn noisy(f32 x) → f32 {
    print x
    return x
}

# 2. call to an ordinary function
@ kernel
@ public
fn calls_host(f32 x) → f32 {
    return host_double(x)
}

# 3. host-only parameter type
@ kernel
@ public
fn takes_list(list<f32> xs) → void {
}

# 4. host call to a private kernel
@ kernel
fn helper(f32 x) → f32 {
    return x + 1.0
}

fn launches_private() → f32 {
    return helper(1.0)
}

# 5. raw lane id
@ kernel
@ public
fn names_its_lane(f32 x) → f32 {
    const vector<u32, 3> gid ← global_invocation_id()
    return x
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.
